conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; helpers: highest(x,n)/lowest(x,n), atr(n), swingHigh(k)/swingLow(k) = k-th most recent confirmed pivot, trendLine(...)/channelLine(...) = projected line value at bar 0

candidates.name: SwingPivot
candidates.quote: The trend channel line will have a similar slope, but draw it between any two swing lows in the bear swing.
candidates.description: Primitive: a swing low is a bar whose low is below the lows of the pivotStrength bars on each side; a swing high is the mirror. Confirmed pivotStrength bars after the pivot bar.
candidates.pseudocode: isSwingLow(i) = low[i] < lowest(low, pivotStrength) over bars i+1..i+pivotStrength && low[i] < lowest(low, pivotStrength) over bars i-pivotStrength..i-1; swingLow(1) = most recent i >= pivotStrength with isSwingLow(i)

complexity.reason: swing-pivot detection with a confirmation lag

candidates.name: TrendLine
candidates.quote: In a bull trend, a trend line is below the lows and a trend channel line is above the highs, and both are rising up and to the right.
candidates.description: The trend line through the two most recent confirmed swing lows (bull) / highs (bear), projected to the current bar.
candidates.pseudocode: p1 = swingLow(2); p2 = swingLow(1); slope = (p2.price - p1.price) / (p2.bar - p1.bar); trendLine[0] = p2.price + slope * (0 - p2.bar)

complexity.reason: line projection from two detected pivots

candidates.name: TrendChannelLineParallelOfTrendLine
candidates.quote: A trend channel line can be created as a parallel of a trend line that is then dragged to the opposite side of the price action... Choose the point that will result in all of the bars between the trend and channel lines being contained between the lines.
candidates.description: The trend channel line is a parallel of the trend line, anchored at the pivot on the opposite side that lies between the trend line's two anchors (so the parallel contains all bars in between). channelLine[0] is its value at bar 0.
candidates.pseudocode: anchor = extreme pivot on the channel side between the trend line's two anchor bars; channelLine[0] = anchor.price + slope * (0 - anchor.bar)

complexity.reason: needs the trend line plus a search for the extreme pivot between its anchors

notes: Brooks also allows drawing the channel line independently, through its own two swing pivots on that side, rather than as a parallel; both constructions are supported by TrendLine (T14-02) applied to the opposite side.

candidates.name: ChannelLineOvershootReversal
candidates.quote: A trend channel line is a useful tool for fading a trend that has gone too far, too fast. Look for an overshoot that reverses, especially if it is the second penetration that is reversing.
candidates.description: Fade at the channel line: the bar's high pokes above the projected bull trend channel line and the bar closes back below it with a bear-reversal quality close; sell at the next open (mirror: buy on a bear channel undershoot).
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] > channelLine[0] && close[0] < channelLine[0] && close[0] < open[0] && (open[0] - close[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick beyond the reversal bar (mechanized: next bar open)

candidates.name: SecondPenetrationPreferredForFade
candidates.quote: especially if it is the second penetration that is reversing.
candidates.description: Prefer the channel-line fade (T14-04) on the second time within lookback bars that the line has been penetrated, rather than the first.

complexity.reason: window count of a derived per-bar penetration flag

candidates.name: SlopingChannelIsOppositeFlag
candidates.quote: In general, any channel that is sloping up to the right can be thought of as a bear flag and it is likely that there will be a breakout through the bottom of the channel... Similarly, a channel that slopes down to the right can be thought of as a bull flag.
candidates.description: Classification: an up-sloping channel is treated as a bear flag (bias toward an eventual downside breakout filter); a down-sloping channel is a bull flag (bias upside).
candidates.pseudocode: slope(trendLine) > 0 -> treat as bear flag; slope(trendLine) < 0 -> treat as bull flag

complexity.reason: needs the trend line's projected slope, itself pivot-dependent

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutOfFallingChannelWithinNBars
candidates.quote: If the market falls through the bottom of a falling channel, the breakout will usually fail within about five bars and lead to a reversal, but it can also be the start of a new, stronger bear leg.
candidates.description: In a falling (bull-flag) channel, a recent close below its trend line within the last failWindowBars followed by a close back above it is a failed-breakout buy; enter at the next open.
candidates.pseudocode: exists i in 1..failWindowBars with close[i] < trendLine[i] && close[0] > trendLine[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the reversal bar (mechanized: next bar open)

complexity.reason: needs the projected trend line evaluated across a small window

candidates.name: WedgeBySlopeComparison
candidates.quote: When a channel has a wedge shape, it is due to urgency. For example, in a wedge top, the slope of the trend line is greater than the slope of the trend channel line.
candidates.description: A rising channel is a wedge (favoring a reversal read) when the trend line's slope exceeds the trend channel line's slope by more than wedgeSlopeMultiple, provided at least two pushes have formed ('what first distinguishes a wedge from a channel is the second pullback').

complexity.reason: needs both projected lines' slopes plus a minimum push count

candidates.name: TwoLegPullbackAfterWedgeReversal
candidates.quote: Traders will see the turn down from the wedge top and most will wait for at least two legs down before they look for the next major pattern to buy or sell.
candidates.description: After a wedge-top reversal (T14-08 fading), require at least a two-legged pullback (two separate down-legs with an intervening bounce) before treating the correction as complete for the next setup.

complexity.reason: 'leg' is not yet defined at the bar level in this chapter; leg counting is fully developed in Chapter 20 and needed here as a prerequisite

candidates.name: RedrawSteeperTrendLineOnSecondPullback
candidates.quote: Once the market turns up, traders can redraw the trend line. Instead of using the parallel of the trend channel line, they now can draw a trend line using the bottoms of the first two pullbacks.
candidates.description: After a second pullback forms, replace the parallel-derived trend line with one drawn directly through the two pullback lows, and compare the market's progress against both the original and the new, steeper channel line to judge whether momentum is accelerating.

complexity.reason: a redraw/replace state machine for which trend line is 'current' is a design decision with no single test

candidates.name: FinalFlagSlopePredictsNewTrendSlope
candidates.quote: One final minor observation is that the slope of the final flag of a trend often provides an approximation of the slope of the new trend.
candidates.description: The slope of the trend/channel line through a trend's final flag can be used as an initial estimate of the slope of the new, opposite-direction trend after a reversal.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context estimate, not a trade trigger)

complexity.reason: requires identifying the 'final flag' -- a pattern-recognition judgment call (book 3 territory) -- before its slope means anything, and Brooks himself calls it 'of limited value'

candidates.name: AnchorSpikeExclusionForChannelLine
candidates.quote: Sometimes there will be a single spike up within an otherwise fairly tight channel, and when that is the case, it is usually best to ignore it and use the other bars for the location of the trend channel line.
candidates.description: Design decision: when selecting the anchor pivot for a trend channel line, exclude an outlier spike bar unless subsequent price action starts respecting the wider line that includes it.
candidates.pseudocode: anchor excludes outlier pivots unless a later bar's high/low tests the wider line derived from the outlier

complexity.reason: 'usually best to ignore it... unless the market decides otherwise' is explicitly a judgment call with no numeric threshold given

rejected.quote: novice traders on the wrong side hold their losing positions until they cannot stand any more pain, and then suddenly all of them exit at once, creating a blow-off or a parabolic climax.
Although you do not need to look at volume when deciding whether to place a trade since it is so unreliable, it is often huge at key turning points, especially at bottoms.
rejected.reason: Brooks explicitly states volume is not needed and is unreliable here; no decidable test is given.

rejected.quote: Every firm uses strategies that they have carefully tested and found to be profitable, but all lose money on 30 to 70 percent of their trades.

chapter_summary: Chapter 14 defines the trend channel line as a parallel of the trend line (or drawn on its own through swing pivots on the far side) and builds the chapter's core countertrend tool: fading an overshoot of the channel line, preferring the second penetration. It adds a slope-based bear-flag/bull-flag classification of any sloping channel, a failed-breakout-within-N-bars rule for a falling channel, and a slope-comparison definition of a wedge. Several ideas (two-legged post-wedge pullback, redrawing a steeper line, final-flag slope as a new-trend estimate, spike-anchor exclusion) are graded research because they depend on primitives not yet built in this book (leg counting, book 3 pattern recognition) or are explicit judgment calls Brooks leaves undefined. Volume and trader-psychology narrative passages were rejected as having no bar-level test.
